Goest
GO-est
v. (2nd pers. sing.)
The second-person singular present of go, formed with the Old English ending -est. Webster 1828 lists it as the archaic inflection used with thou. Its presence in the Authorized Version is not ornament: it marks that one person, not a crowd, is being addressed.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Goest is the form go takes when God or a man speaks to a single person, and the Authorized Version preserves a distinction modern English has lost. Every thou…goest in Scripture is a promise or a demand aimed at one man. God says to Jacob, alone on a stone at Bethel with his brother behind him and a stranger’s house ahead, I am with thee, and will keep thee in all places whither thou goest, and will bring thee again into this land (Genesis 28:15). To Joshua, standing where Moses had stood, the same singular: be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest (Joshua 1:9). The command to be strong is not general encouragement broadcast to a nation; it is laid on one man’s shoulders with a promise attached to his particular movements. Ruth uses the form to bind herself to Naomi: whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge; thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God (Ruth 1:16) — a covenant made by a Moabitess to a bereaved woman with nothing to give her. And a would-be disciple offers it to Christ without counting what it costs: Lord, I will follow thee whithersoever thou goest (Luke 9:57), to which the Lord answered that the Son of man had nowhere to lay His head.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 treats GOEST as the second person singular of the verb go, used with the pronoun thou: thou goest, that is, thou movest, walkest, passest, or proceedest from one place to another.

expand to see more

GOEST — the second person singular, present tense, of the verb GO; used with the pronoun thou.

GO, v.i. — To move, to pass, to proceed from one place, condition, or state to another.

To walk; to move on the feet, as distinguished from riding or being carried.

To depart; to set out on a journey or course; as, whither goest thou?

From Saxon gan, to go — the root also of gone, gait, and gang in its older English sense of going.

Key Scripture

Genesis 28:15 — "And, behold, I am with thee, and will keep thee in all places whither thou goest, and will bring thee again into this land; for I will not leave thee, until I have done that which I have spoken to thee of."

Joshua 1:9 — "Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest."

Ruth 1:16 — "And Ruth said, Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God:"

Luke 9:57 — "And it came to pass, that, as they went in the way, a certain man said unto him, Lord, I will follow thee whithersoever thou goest."

Modern Corruption

Modern English has collapsed the singular thou and the plural ye into one word, and every translation that follows it silently destroys information the Hebrew and Greek carry, so that readers cannot tell whether a promise or a command lands on one person or on the whole congregation.

expand to see more

The loss is not sentimental. In the Authorized Version thou, thee, thy and the verb ending -est are always singular, while ye, you and your are always plural, and the translators used them with mechanical consistency to reproduce a distinction present in both Hebrew and Greek. When Joshua 1:9 says whithersoever thou goest, the reader of the AV knows the promise is to Joshua personally. When the Lord tells Peter Simon, Simon, Satan hath desired to have you and then I have prayed for thee, the AV shows what a modern version cannot: Satan asked for all the disciples, Christ prayed for one man by name. A version that renders both with you has not modernised the sentence; it has deleted the point of it.

The usual reply is that thou is archaic and therefore a barrier, but the archaism is doing work no living English form can do, and the argument proves more than its makers want. The same reasoning would strip the covenant name, the imprecatory psalms, and the genealogies. The dictionary does not hold that the AV’s English is inspired or that other faithful translations may not be used; it holds that where a version discards a distinction the original languages actually make, the reader is poorer and usually does not know it. Recovering the second-person singular forms is one of the plainest arguments for keeping the Authorized Version in the hands of the people who study.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew halak (H1980), to go, to walk, to proceed; yatsa (H3318), to go out; Greek poreuomai (G4198), to go, to journey; hupago (G5217), to go away, to depart.

expand to see more

Hebrew halak (H1980) — to go, to walk; the great Old Testament verb of both travel and moral conduct (Genesis 28:15; Micah 6:8).

Hebrew yatsa (H3318) — to go out, go forth; used of armies, of the word of the LORD, and of a man leaving his house.

Greek poreuomai (G4198) — to go, to proceed, to journey; whithersoever thou goest (Luke 9:57).

Greek hupago (G5217) — to withdraw, to go away; the Lord’s word for His own departure to the Father (John 16:5).

Greek peripateo (G4043) — to walk about; the New Testament equivalent of halak in its moral sense (Ephesians 4:1).

Usage

"I will keep thee in all places whither thou goest (Genesis 28:15) — a promise to one fugitive man."

"The LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest (Joshua 1:9) — the courage commanded rests on the presence promised."

"Whither thou goest, I will go (Ruth 1:16) — a Moabitess binding herself to Israel’s God."
